summary: Subnetting splits an IP network into smaller networks by borrowing host bits for the network part. With CIDR the boundary can be at any bit, written as a prefix length such as /26.

sections.heading: Prefix notation
sections.body: A CIDR address is an IP address followed by a slash and the number of leading network bits (RFC 4632). 192.168.1.0/26 has 26 network bits and 6 host bits.

sections.heading: The four numbers you compute
bullets: Broadcast address: all host bits set to 1.
Usable hosts: 2^h - 2, where h is the number of host bits.

sections.heading: Worked example: 192.168.1.130/26
sections.body: A /26 has block size 64 in the last octet (256 - 192). Blocks start at 0, 64, 128, 192. The address 130 falls in the block starting at 128.

sections.heading: Dividing a network
sections.body: To split 192.168.1.0/24 into four equal subnets, borrow 2 bits: /26. The subnets are .0/26, .64/26, .128/26, .192/26, each with 62 usable hosts.

sections.heading: Special prefixes
bullets: /31: point-to-point links with two usable addresses (RFC 3021).

subtopics.title: VLSM
subtopics.summary: Different sized subnets from one block.

sections.body: Variable Length Subnet Masks let you give each segment only what it needs: allocate the largest subnet first, then carve smaller ones from what remains. Example: 10.0.0.0/24 into a /25 for 100 hosts, a /26 for 50, and /30s for router links.
Contiguous, aligned blocks collapse into one shorter prefix: 192.168.0.0/24 and 192.168.1.0/24 become 192.168.0.0/23. Aggregation shrinks routing tables and is the point of CIDR.

Find the interesting octet, compute block size = 256 - mask value in that octet, then find the multiple of the block size at or below the address. That multiple is the network; the next multiple minus one is the broadcast.

A host ANDs the destination with its own mask; if the result equals its own network, it ARPs for the destination directly, otherwise it sends to the default gateway. A wrong mask breaks this decision and causes odd one-way connectivity.

takeaways: CIDR /n = n network bits; host bits h = 32 - n.
Block size in the interesting octet = 256 - mask value.
VLSM allocates by need; aggregation shortens routing tables.
